n: What if a murder victim is found in the countryside and no one knows who did it? Innocent blood still defiles the land, so the community must respond.

f.w: it be not known who hath slain him

n: Leaders measured the distance to nearby towns to determine which one bore responsibility.
The nearest town’s elders took a young cow that had never been worked.

f.g: A young cow that has not yet calved.

f.w: which hath not been wrought with

n: In an untilled valley with flowing water, they broke the heifer’s neck. The animal’s death stood in place of the unknown killer’s.

f.g: Possibly “a valley with an ever-flowing stream.”

n: Priests attended, because they represented God and had authority to settle disputes and pronounce blessings.

f.g: Every dispute and every case of assault.

n: The elders washed their hands over the heifer — a public sign of innocence. Pilate later used the same gesture.
They declared under oath that they neither committed nor witnessed the crime.

f.w: Our hands have not shed this blood

n: They prayed for God’s mercy on the nation he had redeemed. Atonement for guilt ultimately comes from God’s mercy.

f.w: the blood shall be forgiven them

n: This rite removed bloodguilt from the community when they obeyed God.

f.w: put away the guilt of innocent blood

n: A new topic: women captured in war (from distant cities, not Canaan).
An Israelite soldier might want to marry a captive woman. The law regulated this so she was not merely used.

f.g: As a legal wife, not a slave.

n: She shaved her head and trimmed her nails — likely signs of mourning and of leaving her old life.
She was given a full month to grieve her parents before the marriage. The law slowed a soldier’s impulse and gave her dignity.

f.w: bewail her father and her mother

n: If the marriage failed, she must be released as a free woman — never sold as a slave. She had rights.

f.g: You have dishonored or taken advantage of her.
Treat her as property to sell.

n: Families with more than one wife had rivalries, as with Jacob, Leah, and Rachel. The law addressed the inheritance problem this created.

f.g: Hebrew idiom: one loved more and one loved less.

n: A father could not give the firstborn’s rights to a favorite wife’s son if he wasn’t truly the firstborn.
The real firstborn received a double share of the inheritance. Favoritism could not override justice.
A grave case: a persistently rebellious son who rejects his parents’ discipline. Parents together share responsibility.
The parents could not punish him themselves; they had to bring him to the elders at the city gate. This limited parental power.

f.g: The city gate, where the court met.

n: Both parents testify. The son is not merely disobedient as a child; he is a destructive adult who wastes the family’s resources.
The punishment was death by stoning. Jewish tradition records few or no cases where it was carried out; the law emphasized how seriously the family and community were protected.
After an execution, a criminal’s body might be hung up publicly as a warning.

f.g: Display the body after death, not hanging as the method of execution.

n: The body must be buried the same day. Paul applied “he that is hanged is accursed” to Christ, who took our curse upon himself on the cross.

f.w: he that is hanged is accursed of God
